name: Ibokun Sign Language
world_status: accessible description is silent on stress

earlier_scan.note: Sign language; only source is Asonye & Akpan 2021 on numeral gestures (minimal); word stress inapplicable/undescribed

sources.citation: Asonye, Emma & Aniefon Daniel Akpan. 2021. Gesture in numerals in three indigenous Nigerian Sign Languages. Slides (27 pp.), 7th International Conference on Language Documentation and Conservation (ICLDC 7), University of Hawai'i, 6 March 2021. http://hdl.handle.net/10125/74462
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.note: Nothing. Only Ibokun-specific content: 'IBOKUN Sign Language is signed in Ibokun village in Obokun Local Govt., Osun State, Nigeria. The village has an estimated population of over 200 Deaf signers, some of whom are bilingual.' plus numeral handshapes (index/pinky finger dominance interchanged relative to Akure SL; B-hand [+OPEN] [+FRONT] for fives; palms join with toes to count from 15 up). No prosody, timing, movement or stress-like statement; Glottolog codes it listed by Glottolog as a minimal description.

sources.citation: Asonye, Emma. 2021. The genocide of signed languages: protecting the linguistic rights of Africa's deaf children. The Conversation, 22 September 2021. doi:10.64628/aaj.wj5tfkqjy
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.note: Nothing; opinion piece on deaf children's linguistic rights, no mention of Ibokun.

sources.citation: Asonye, Emmanuel Ihechi, Ezinne Emma-Asonye & Mary Edward. 2018. Deaf in Nigeria: A preliminary survey of isolated deaf communities. SAGE Open 8(2). doi:10.1177/2158244018786538
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.note: Nothing about Ibokun: the survey covers deaf communities in Abuja and Imo; a full-text search for stress/accent the full text finds no 'Ibokun', 'Obokun' or 'Osun' and no 'stress'/'prosod'. Only general remark that the school sign language 'relies on the four articulatory parameters proposed by Stokoe (1960) and Liddell and Johnson (1989) for its phonological description'.
